close.title: Everyone counts 45 days from the invoice date.
close.body: That's the wrong date — and we can show you exactly what it costs.

beats.caption: Since FY24, if you pay a registered small supplier late, you don't just owe interest — you lose the tax deduction on that purchase for the whole year.
Five lakh invoice, twenty-five percent tax: one and a quarter lakh gone, purely because of when you paid. Forty-five days if there's a contract, fifteen if there isn't.
Almost nobody tracks it, because the hard part was never counting to forty-five. It's knowing which suppliers it applies to, and when the clock actually started.
So we built Ledgr. Three things, sitting on top of your unpaid bills.

It works out which of your suppliers the law actually reaches. Then on every bill it works out the real deadline, flags what's about to breach, and pays through RazorpayX before it does. And it looks backwards — what last year already cost you.
The two hard parts there are judgement, not arithmetic. Which supplier. And which date. That's where the AI is — and it's the only place it is.
One decision matters more than the rest, so I'll show you that rather than the whole diagram.
Two agents do the reading — contracts, delivery notes, email threads — and report what they found, with the evidence attached.

But they decide nothing. Two hardcoded rules do that: does the law apply, and what's the deadline. The agents can't produce a deadline — that field doesn't exist in what they submit, and there's a test asserting it.
So the model can be wrong about something it read, and you'll see that on screen with its source. It can't be wrong about the answer.
Twenty-four suppliers. Which of them does the law actually cover? Sixteen in scope, six not, and two it won't answer.
Registered, small, active — everything a simple check looks for. And still the wrong answer, because Orion is a registered wholesale trader, and trade sits outside this obligation.
Left, what the agent found. Right, the rule that decided, showing its working.
And this one it refuses. Nothing declared, nothing in the registry. Unresolved — not not-covered. Guessing there quietly loses a real deduction.
That's today. This is last year — a hundred and eighty-five invoices.
Twenty-nine lakh of exposure. And ninety-three lakh it excluded — payments a naive check would have had you chasing for nothing.

beats.caption: One live. Two lakh, accepted today, from a registered small supplier.
Out of scope. Orion is a trader.
Same amount, same dates. Only the supplier changes.
Forty-five day deadline, fifty thousand of exposure. Nothing about the money changed.
Five lakh, over our auto-execute threshold, so it needs a person. This is a real RazorpayX payout call.
Watch this. The row hasn't closed. It's asking me to confirm.
That's deliberate. A payout being requested isn't a compliance item being closed. It closes when RazorpayX confirms the money moved.
Now it's closed. Under ten thousand goes automatically. Above it, always a human.

beats.caption: This is the question I'd ask if I were sitting where you are.

beats.section: 9 · Does the AI earn its place?
beats.caption: Same pipeline twice. Once with the agents, once with string matching and no model. Same data, same scoring, both against answers we know are right.

beats.section: 9 · Does the AI earn its place?
beats.caption: String matching gets twenty of twenty-four suppliers. The agent gets twenty-four. On last year's ledger the simple version misreads fifty-nine invoices — over a crore. The agent misreads eight.

beats.section: 9 · Does the AI earn its place?
beats.caption: And the three it wrongly calls covered? Forty-five lakh you would have rushed for nothing.
